summary:
Brian John, a Principal Full Stack Engineer at BetterUp focused on AI enablement for R&D, presents a technique for adding subagent capabilities to Codex CLI, which natively lacks this feature. His primary motivation is avoiding vendor lock-in: he uses Claude Code as his daily driver and relies heavily on subagents for context management, where a main agent delegates problems to subagents that consume tokens and return only answers, keeping the main context window clean. He references Dex Hory's talk on AI workflows as influential.

The design is straightforward: a parent Codex session runs a wrapper script that identifies which agent to execute, builds the prompt, and kicks off a child Codex process via codex exec. The child subagent does its work, writes results to a file, and the wrapper script reads that file and returns the output to the parent session via stdout. The hardest part proved to be determining minimum required sandbox permissions. The parent needs at least sandbox workspace write to run the codex command. The child process is trickier: it needs sandbox workspace write to write output files, must have rollout recorder disabled, and cannot access OpenAI credentials in the home directory since they fall outside the workspace. A wrapper around codex syncs home directory files into a subdirectory and sets CODEX_HOME accordingly.

John references Meta's "agents rule of two" paper for security framing, noting three risk factors: untrustworthy input, access to sensitive data, and ability to change state or communicate externally. He classifies his setup as lower risk but cautions that lower risk does not mean no risk. Configuration is done through agents.md, which tells Codex how and when to run subagents and what agents are available. Each agent definition includes a name, reasoning effort level (light/medium/high), and a prompt.

A key design decision is writing the agent name and user query to files rather than passing them as command arguments. This exploits Codex's permissioning system: if the command looks identical each time, permission is granted once; varying arguments require repeated approval. The demo showcases two toy agents (word counter and file writer), a 72-line wrapper script, and an agent executor Python class. Limitations include Codex's serial execution (no async like Claude Code), slower overall performance, and potentially long agent runtimes (up to 20 minutes), necessitating generous timeouts (600 seconds in the demo).
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Brian John introduces himself as a Principal Full Stack Engineer at BetterUp focused on AI enablement for R&D. He explains his motivation: he uses Claude Code as his daily driver with subagents but wants to avoid lock-in to one tool or model family. He wants to use Codex CLI with subagents to port his workflows. He highlights context management as a key subagent benefit and credits Dex Hory's talk on AI workflows as influential.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: John describes the subagent design: a parent Codex session runs a wrapper script that determines which agent to run, builds the prompt, and kicks off codex exec. The child Codex runs as the subagent, does its work, writes its answer to a file, and the wrapper script reads that file and prints the result to stdout for the parent session.

sections.title: Sandbox Permission Challenges
sections.summary: Getting the right permissions was the hardest part. The parent needs at least sandbox workspace write to run the codex command. The child process is trickier: the sandbox blocks access to OpenAI credentials in the home directory, needs workspace write to write output files, and requires disabling the rollout recorder. John notes he avoids running with dangerously skip permissions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.summary: John references Meta's 'agents rule of two' paper, which identifies three security factors: processing untrustworthy input, access to sensitive systems or private data, and ability to change state or communicate externally. He classifies his setup as lower risk since it doesn't process untrustworthy input, the state changes are low risk, and external communication is only to OpenAI's API. He cautions that lower risk does not mean no risk.

sections.title: Configuration via Agents.md
sections.summary: John explains that agents.md tells Codex how to run subagents (which script and commands to use), when to run them (when user asks or when helpful), and what subagents are available and what they do.

sections.title: Demo: Agent Definitions and Code Walkthrough
sections.summary: John walks through his proof-of-concept repository. Agent definitions include a name, reasoning effort (light/medium/high), and prompt. He shows the 72-line wrapper script, the agent executor Python class, and explains the key design decision to write agent name and query to files rather than pass as arguments to avoid repeated permission prompts. He also shows a wrapper around codex that syncs home directory files and sets CODEX_HOME.

sections.title: Live Demo Execution
sections.summary: John launches the system and demonstrates two subagents: a word counter and a file writer. He shows Codex writing agent name and query to files, requesting permission once, and returning results. He notes Codex runs serially (no async like Claude Code), uses a 600-second timeout for potentially long-running agents, and that the word counter took about 40 seconds.

sections.title: Conclusion and Contact Info
sections.summary: John points to the open-source repository URL, mentions BetterUp's website, and provides his email and X handle for questions. He encourages viewers to reach out if BetterUp sounds like an interesting place to work.
